title: Resting heart rate outside your usual range
meaning: Most adults at rest have a heart rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute, and your own normal matters most. A fast pulse can signal dehydration or an infection, and any change from your normal can point to a health problem.
actions: Sit still for 10 minutes, then check again
Drink some water: dehydration is one cause
Think about how much you slept, ate and drank today
Tell the flight surgeon if it stays outside your usual range

sources.title: MedlinePlus, Pulse (reviewed 1/1/2025)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 027: Water, p. 2

title: Resting heart rate far outside the safe range
meaning: Your resting heart rate is far from the typical 60 to 100 beats per minute.
actions: Sit down and rest
Check again after 10 minutes of rest
Contact the flight surgeon

sources.title: MedlinePlus, Pulse (reviewed 1/1/2025)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 044: Medical Operations, p. 16: medical decisions lie with the crew surgeon

title: Blood oxygen a little low
meaning: A reading of 93 or 94, or lower than your usual, is a reason to ask a doctor for advice. A cold hand, nail varnish or movement can give a false low reading, and low oxygen in the cabin air can also cause it.
actions: Rest, warm your hand and keep still, then measure again
Check the cabin air readings and alarms
Tell the flight surgeon if it stays at 93 or 94, or lower than your usual

sources.title: NHS England, Using a pulse oximeter to check you are OK (2022), pp. 6-7, 16
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, pp. 5-6

title: Low blood oxygen
meaning: A reading that stays at 92% or less needs urgent medical help. In a spacecraft it can also mean a problem with the cabin air.
actions: Measure again straight away with a warm, still hand
Check the cabin air readings and alarms
If you also feel tired, sick, dizzy or have a headache, put on an oxygen mask: crew are trained to do this at any sign of low oxygen
Contact the flight surgeon now

sources.title: NHS England, Using a pulse oximeter to check you are OK (2022), pp. 12-13
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, pp. 3, 5

title: Skin temperature outside the usual range
meaning: Forehead skin temperature is not core body temperature. In one study of 1,000 healthy adults the normal forehead range was about 31.0 to 35.6 °C, and readings above 35.6 °C suggested a fever. The room, exercise or a cold forehead can change a reading.
actions: Rest for a few minutes in a comfortable room, then measure again
Drink some water
Tell the flight surgeon if you also feel unwell or it does not improve

sources.title: Ng et al. 2005, Am J Infect Control 33(4):227-229: normal forehead temperature by handheld infrared thermometer
NHS, High temperature (fever) in adults (reviewed 19 Oct 2026)

title: Skin temperature at fever level
meaning: A temperature of 38 °C or above is usually considered a fever.
actions: Rest, then measure again
Drink some water
Contact the flight surgeon

sources.title: NHS, High temperature (fever) in adults (reviewed 19 Oct 2026)

title: Blood pressure outside your usual range
meaning: At home, 135/85 or higher is usually considered high, and below 90/60 is considered low. Low blood pressure can cause dizziness, feeling sick, blurred vision, weakness, confusion or fainting. One reading is not a diagnosis.
actions: Sit still for 5 minutes, then measure again on the same arm
Note any dizziness, feeling sick, blurred vision, confusion or fainting
Tell the flight surgeon if your readings stay outside the range or you keep having these symptoms

sources.title: NHS, High blood pressure (reviewed 19 July 2024)
NHS, Low blood pressure (hypotension) (reviewed 11 July 2023)

title: Very high blood pressure
meaning: A reading above 180 (top number) and/or above 120 (bottom number) is severe. With chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, a change in vision or difficulty speaking it is an emergency.
actions: Sit still for 5 minutes, then measure again
Contact the flight surgeon now
If you have chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, a change in vision or difficulty speaking, press 'I feel unwell now'

sources.title: CDC, About High Blood Pressure (updated 13 Oct 2026)
NHS, High blood pressure (reviewed 19 July 2024)

title: Blood sugar outside the usual range
meaning: For a fasting reading, 99 mg/dL or below is normal and 100 to 125 is in the prediabetes range. Below 70 mg/dL is low, which can bring a racing heart, shaking, sweating, dizziness, hunger or confusion.
actions: Check you measured before eating, as your meter instructs
Measure again
Tell the flight surgeon: a doctor may want to re-test to be sure
If you feel shaky, sweaty, dizzy or confused, tell a crewmate

sources.title: CDC, Diabetes Testing (15 May 2024)
CDC, Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (16 May 2024)

title: Blood sugar far outside the usual range
meaning: A fasting reading of 126 mg/dL or above is in the diabetes range, and below 54 mg/dL is severe low blood sugar.
actions: Measure again
Contact the flight surgeon now
If you have a seizure, faint or are confused, press 'I feel unwell now'

sources.title: CDC, Diabetes Testing (15 May 2024)
CDC, Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (16 May 2024)

title: Less sleep than you need
meaning: Adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Astronauts sleep about 6 hours on average in space, and NASA warns that sleep loss slows thinking, memory and judgement, and can affect mood and health.
actions: Keep your sleep space cool, dark and quiet
Avoid caffeine for 6 to 12 hours before sleep
Avoid bright and blue light for 1 to 2 hours before bed
Avoid vigorous exercise and large or spicy meals within 2 hours of sleep
Skip daytime naps unless your schedule includes one
Ask the flight surgeon for advice if sleep problems continue

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 041: Sleep Accommodations, pp. 3, 5, 7-8
NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief 009: Circadian Desynchrony, pp. 3-4

title: Feeling low
meaning: Stress, low mood and anxiety are common in spaceflight. They can pass with time or support, or grow into something that needs care. Sleep, workload, low oxygen, food and carbon dioxide can all contribute.
actions: Talk to a crewmate or someone you trust
Ask the flight surgeon for a private psychological conference: NASA provides them
Try journaling or photographing Earth: NASA lists both as ways astronauts manage stress
Check your sleep, food and water today

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 016: Behavioral Health, pp. 3, 6-7, 14

title: Low water intake today
meaning: ISS crews drank about 2 to 2.3 litres a day, and NASA plans at least 2.5 litres per crew member per day, including water used to rehydrate food. Too little water can reduce concentration and physical performance, and cause headache, sleepiness and less urine.
actions: Drink water regularly through the day
Limit alcohol and caffeine: NASA lists them as causes of dehydration
Drink more after exercise lasting over 60 minutes
Tell the flight surgeon if you have a headache, confusion or much less urine

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 027: Water, pp. 2-4

title: Not enough exercise today
meaning: In microgravity bones and muscles carry less load, which reduces bone density and can raise the risk of fracture. Exercise is NASA's first line of defence: earlier crew requirements were 2 hours per workday.
actions: Do today's planned exercise session
Resistance exercise that loads the bones works best
Ask the exercise specialists to adjust your programme
Keep eating and drinking enough: nutrition also protects bone

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief 013: Bone Loss, pp. 2, 8, 12, 14
WHO, Physical activity fact sheet (4 Nov 2026)

title: Skipped meals
meaning: NASA links too little food in space to weight loss, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and weaker immune function, and notes that skipped meals can happen when meal times are not kept.
actions: Eat your planned meals, even if you are not hungry
Drink water with your food
If nausea or space sickness stops you eating, tell the flight surgeon: controlling it is essential for a healthy appetite

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 013: Food and Nutrition, pp. 3, 12

title: Feeling dizzy
meaning: Dizziness has many causes. After spaceflight, standing up can cause light-headedness or fainting because blood pressure is harder to keep up. Low oxygen in the cabin air, dehydration and low blood pressure can also cause it. This is guidance, not a diagnosis.
actions: If you feel faint, lie down with your legs raised, or sit with your head lowered between your knees
Drink some water
Check the cabin air alarms; put on an oxygen mask if you think the air is the cause
Tell a crewmate and the flight surgeon
If you faint, press 'I feel unwell now'

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 019: Orthostatic Intolerance, pp. 1, 3
NHS, Fainting (reviewed 17 Aug 2026)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, pp. 3, 5

title: Feeling sick
meaning: Nausea is common in the first days of spaceflight: space adaptation sickness affects 70 to 90% of crew, usually starts in the first 3 to 7 days and lasts 2 to 3 days or longer. Low oxygen in the cabin, dehydration and food-borne illness can also cause it.
actions: Limit head movements and avoid sudden turns
Get more air moving around you
Stay hydrated
Restrict your activity, close your eyes or concentrate on a task
Tell the flight surgeon if it is severe or lasts more than a few days

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief 004: Space Adaptation Sickness, pp. 1-2, 6-8
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, p. 5
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 013: Food and Nutrition, p. 18

title: Headache
meaning: Headaches are very common in the first days of spaceflight (reported by up to 90% of astronauts), and can also come from low oxygen or dehydration. A headache that starts suddenly and is extremely painful, or comes with numbness, weakness, confusion, trouble speaking or loss of vision, is an emergency.
actions: Drink some water
Rest in a quiet place
Check the cabin air alarms
Tell the flight surgeon if it keeps coming back or gets worse
If it started suddenly and is extremely painful, or you have the signs above, press 'I feel unwell now'

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief 004: Space Adaptation Sickness, p. 3
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, p. 5
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 027: Water, p. 2
NHS, Headaches (reviewed 17 Apr 2024)

title: Feeling very tired
meaning: Tiredness is common and has many causes: too little sleep, food or water, stress, and low oxygen in the cabin, which NASA notes can be mistaken for fatigue.
actions: Think about how much you slept, ate and drank today
Check the cabin air alarms if you are unusually tired
Rest if you can
Tell the flight surgeon if it lasts for several days

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 041: Sleep Accommodations, p. 3
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, p. 6
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 027: Water, p. 2

title: Feeling feverish
meaning: A temperature of 38 °C or above is usually considered a fever. NASA lists influenza and other infections among the conditions seen in flight, and food-borne illness can cause fever, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
actions: Measure your temperature with the station
Rest and drink water
Tell the flight surgeon: contact them urgently if it is not improving or is getting worse

sources.title: NHS, High temperature (fever) in adults (reviewed 19 Oct 2026)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 033: Spaceflight Experience and Medical Care, p. 13
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 013: Food and Nutrition, p. 18

title: Skin rash
meaning: A rash can have many causes. A rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it needs emergency help.
actions: Roll a clear glass or cup over the rash: if it does not fade, press 'I feel unwell now'
Otherwise tell the flight surgeon
Photographs of skin changes can help the doctors: NASA uses skin photo-documentation

sources.title: NHS England, Using a pulse oximeter to check you are OK (2022), p. 14
NHS, Headaches (reviewed 17 Apr 2024)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 043: Longitudinal Health Surveillance, p. 3

title: Sore throat or cold sore
meaning: NASA says the immune system can be affected by the stress of long missions, and lists throat infections (pharyngitis) among conditions seen in flight.
actions: Rest and drink water
Check your temperature with the morning check
Tell the flight surgeon about new symptoms: they keep your health record

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 033: Spaceflight Experience and Medical Care, p. 13
NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C (crew health standard), p. 35 and V1 7001

title: Vision changes
meaning: Some astronauts get vision changes on long missions: NASA calls it SANS, eye changes linked to fluid shifting towards the head. About 16% of crew show swelling of the optic disc, most of it mild. Low oxygen can also dim colour, night and side vision.
actions: Tell the flight surgeon about any change in vision
NASA can provide glasses with stronger lenses if needed
Check the cabin air alarms
Eye checks are part of your scheduled health exams

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 033: Spaceflight Experience and Medical Care, p. 5
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, p. 5
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 043: Longitudinal Health Surveillance, p. 4
NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C (crew health standard), V1 3004 g
